title: Michael Burry Says This Rally Is Detached From Reality
excerpt: The 'Big Short' investor warns AI euphoria has pushed markets to dot-com-era extremes, urging investors to cut exposure now.
body:
Michael Burry, the investor who called the 2008 housing collapse, published a stark warning on May 8 — the same day the S&P 500 hit another record high — telling investors the market's relentless AI-driven advance has lost touch with fundamentals.

**What Burry said:**
Burry wrote that 'stocks are not up or down because of jobs or consumer sentiment' — they are 'going straight up because they have been going straight up,' on a 'two-letter thesis that everyone thinks they understand,' leaving him feeling like this is 'the last months of the 1999-2000 bubble.' His prescription was blunt: he urged investors to 'simply reduce exposure to stocks, to tech stocks in particular' and for 'any stocks going parabolic reduce positions almost entirely.'

**Why this warning carries weight:**
Burry has been warning for months that the stock market's AI fixation increasingly resembles the final stages of the dot-com bubble. Supporting data backs his unease: as of May 8, 2026, the Buffett Indicator — which compares total U.S. stock market capitalization to GDP — stood at 229.9, significantly above its 20-year average of 128.25. The Shiller CAPE ratio stood at 40.1, near levels seen only at the peak of the dot-com bubble.

**The honest caveat:**
The pattern with Burry suggests he tends to be right about the diagnosis but early on the timing — the bubble comparison may prove accurate without offering any reliable signal about when the correction arrives. Burry himself acknowledged that directly betting against the rally through short selling is risky and impractical for most investors, particularly as bearish trades have become increasingly expensive.

**What to watch:**
Watch whether institutional fund managers begin trimming tech exposure in their next quarterly filings — that shift, more than any single Substack post, will signal whether Wall Street is finally listening.
